When you describe food as braised, you are saying that it was cooked using a specific two-step method — first seared in hot fat, then slowly cooked in a small amount of liquid inside a covered pot. The word tells you both how the food was prepared and, as a result, what it is like to eat.
The Two Steps That Make Something "Braised"

Step 1 — Searing (the dry part):
The food, usually a large piece of meat or a hearty vegetable, is placed in a pot with a little oil or butter over high heat. It sits there, untouched, until its outer surface turns deep brown and develops a crust. This is not about cooking the inside — it is about building flavor and color on the outside. This step is called searing or browning.

Step 2 — Slow cooking in liquid (the wet part):
After searing, a modest amount of liquid is poured into the same pot. This liquid could be water, stock, wine, beer, or a mixture. Crucially, the liquid does not fully cover the food — it typically comes only partway up its sides. The pot is then tightly covered with a lid, and the heat is turned down very low. The food then cooks slowly for a long time — often anywhere from one to several hours — inside this sealed, steamy environment.

This combination is what braising is. The word "braised" is the adjective form that tells you the food went through this exact process.
Why This Method Is Used — and What It Does to the Food

Braising is not chosen randomly. It is specifically designed for ingredients that would become tough, dry, or chewy if cooked quickly — most often tough cuts of meat, such as the shoulder, shank, ribs, or brisket of an animal. These cuts contain a lot of connective tissue (the tough, fibrous material that holds muscles together). Under normal, quick cooking, this tissue stays tough and makes the meat rubbery.

But under the long, moist, gentle heat of braising, something important happens: the connective tissue slowly breaks down and dissolves into a rich, silky substance called gelatin. This is what makes braised meat fall apart tenderly, almost melting in your mouth, rather than being chewy.

Meanwhile, the liquid in the pot absorbs all the flavors released from the meat and the browned crust. By the time the food is done, this liquid has reduced and concentrated into a deeply flavorful sauce — often glossy and rich — that is usually served alongside or over the food.
What Braised Food Looks, Feels, and Tastes Like

When you encounter something described as braised, you can expect:

  • Extremely tender texture. It pulls apart easily — sometimes with just a fork or spoon. It does not require a knife.
  • Moist and juicy interior. It is never dry. The long cooking in a covered pot keeps moisture inside.
  • Deep, rich, complex flavor. The combination of the initial browning and the slow absorption of liquid creates layers of savory taste that quick-cooked food simply cannot achieve.
  • A flavorful, reduced sauce. The cooking liquid left in the pot is not discarded — it becomes a sauce, broth, or gravy that carries concentrated flavor.

Almost any food can technically be braised, but the method is most commonly and most usefully applied to:

  • Tough cuts of red meat: beef short ribs, beef brisket, lamb shanks, pork shoulder, oxtail, veal cheeks
  • Poultry with darker, fattier meat: chicken thighs and legs (rather than lean breast meat, which does not benefit as much)
  • Firm vegetables: cabbage, fennel, leeks, endive, celery root — vegetables that hold their shape but become wonderfully soft and sweet after slow, moist cooking

Lean, tender cuts (like a chicken breast or a beef tenderloin) are generally not braised, because they do not have the tough connective tissue that braising is designed to break down. Cooking them this way would make them dry and stringy.
How the Adjective Is Used in Context

The word "braised" sits directly before the name of the food it describes, telling you how that food was cooked:

  • "I ordered the braised short ribs." → Short ribs that were seared and then slow-cooked in liquid until fall-apart tender.
  • "The menu had braised lamb shanks with root vegetables." → Lamb shanks prepared by the two-step braising method.
  • "She made braised cabbage as a side dish." → Cabbage that was browned and then slowly cooked in a little liquid until soft and flavorful.
  • "The braised pork shoulder took four hours to make." → Pork shoulder cooked low and slow in a covered pot after searing.

In every case, "braised" signals the same thing: the food was first seared for flavor and color, then covered and gently cooked in liquid for a long time, resulting in something tender, moist, and deeply savory.

If you had to hold onto just one idea: braised food is food that was browned first, then slowly cooked in a small amount of liquid inside a covered pot until it becomes tender and rich. The adjective "braised" carries all of that meaning in a single word — it tells you the method, and it promises you a result that is soft, juicy, and full of deep flavor.
